summary: Round 5, one added line: the rounds:M4.38 cap argument in baselines/review.txt. No code, no tests; the three surviving-mutation claims and the rows' substance are CARRIED FORWARD from rounds 2, 3 and 4, not re-run, as instructed. What I did check is every claim the new line makes about measurements I performed, against my own artifacts in .harness/review. All of them hold. (1) 'measured both ways, CountDownLatch survives and Semaphore.acquireUninterruptibly kills' is verbatim what I recorded at 9a50b5d0/T3 -- latch pin: queuedCallerFreedWithin4s=true both unmutated and with close():459 deleted, mutation SURVIVES; same probe with Semaphore.acquireUninterruptibly: freed unmutated, never freed mutated, mutation KILLED in ~150 ms. The 'I' in that sentence attaches to 'had written', not to 'measured', so nothing is claimed for the author that a reviewer ran. (2) 'the release issues putIfMatch, which opens no channel and completes with the flag still set, while only putIfAbsent, the ACQUIRE path, throws; both reviewers measured it independently' matches my a6f08958/T1 (putIfMatch completes with flag pre-set and still set, platform and virtual thread, three runs each, JDK 25.0.4) and the production reviewer's independent probe in M4.38-R3-1, re-run again at b699a7d0. Independence is real: two probes, two records, neither citing the other. (3) 'a latch would serve there is still false and both reviewers caught it' is accurate -- my b699a7d0/T1 and the production reviewer's M4.38-R4-1, same clause, same round, raised separately. (4) The no-convergence claim is HONEST, not self-flattering: findings did not shrink, round 4 carried the MOST minors of any round, the entry names the author's own drafting rather than the reviewers as the cause, and 'I should have stopped after round 2' is supported by the artifacts -- round 2 passed both roles, and round 3's major was CREATED by the redraft that followed it, promoting the round-2 production reviewer's own explicitly-unmeasured R2-5 into M4.35 as fact. '17 inserted lines across three docs files' checks out exactly (1+13+3). Four minors, all about hand-carried counts and one date, none blocking, none worth a round to fix.

findings.title: The entry hand-carries four counts; two are wrong against the artifacts, in a file whose neighbouring entries say not to hand-carry counts
findings.detail: M0.53's and M4.7a's entries in this same file both say 'the count is left to review_rounds.py, because a count carried by hand in prose is stale by the round after it'. This entry carries four. (a) 'Round 4 passed both roles with four minors': each ROLE returned four, but the union is FIVE distinct prose defects -- shared: the 'a latch would serve there' clause (my T1 / their R4-1), the backslash-escaped quotes (my T4 / their R4-2), the same measurement recorded with two different ranges (my T3 / their R4-4); unique to me: M4.35's leading INTERLEAVING paragraph being stale after the correction that follows it (T2); unique to the production reviewer: 'Neither backend that exists has it' being false under its nearest antecedent (R4-3). (b) 'every round found a defect in PROSE, in the same three paragraphs' -- four paragraphs carried defects, not three: M4.35, M4.36, the done row, and M4.37, whose row was cited by name in the production reviewer's R2-3 (backlog-notes.md:305, the measurement attached to the floor). (c) 'THREE CLAUSE-ATTACHMENT ERRORS' is defensible under a reasonable grouping (M4.35's round-1 backwards clause, R3-1's 'whose ...begin()' attaching to putIfAbsent, R3-2's 'which' attaching to the margin) but excludes R4-3, which is the same family; it is at risk of being an undercount by one. (d) 'twice in sentences written to fix the previous one' is exactly right and is the one figure I could verify without ambiguity. The argument the entry is making survives every one of these -- a per-row split still puts each row's prose in front of the same reviewer -- which is why this is minor.
findings.failure_scenario: The reading that matters is (a). The commit body is where these minors are supposed to survive, and this entry tells whoever writes it there are four. If four are transcribed, one of the two role-unique minors -- most likely mine, M4.35's stale interleaving paragraph, since the three shared ones are the memorable ones -- is recorded nowhere at all. That is precisely the failure the production reviewer measured at R2-4 against an earlier draft of these very rows: the 'awaitSet polls where a latch would be exact' minor was declared recorded-not-fixed and then 'appears nowhere under docs/ after this commit and therefore does NOT survive'. This commit exists to stop review findings evaporating into commit bodies nothing loads; losing one to its own count would be the same defect one level up.

findings.title: 'The second instance came two hours after I had written up the lesson from the first' is contradicted by the entry's own anchoring -- the window is at most 17 minutes
findings.detail: The entry anchors both instances itself: 'ROUNDS 2 AND 3 WERE THE SAME ERROR TWICE'. The lesson from the first instance cannot have been written before the first instance was FOUND, which is my round-2 verdict, recorded 02:47 (.harness/review/9a50b5d0...test-reviewer.json; the production reviewer's R2-2 followed at 02:54). The second instance -- M4.35's ClosedByInterruptException sentence -- was in the draft reviewed at round 3, recorded 03:04/03:05 (a6f08958...). So the whole interval from 'lesson available to be written up' to 'second instance written' is 02:47 to 03:04, seventeen minutes, and the redraft itself occupied ten of them. The entire M4.38 review history spans 02:31 to 03:18; no two hours exist anywhere in it. I cannot see the author's transcript and am not looking for it, so I cannot say what 'two hours' is a memory of -- only that under the entry's own anchoring it is false by an order of magnitude.
findings.failure_scenario: The sentence exists to make one point: enough time passed for the lesson to have been absorbed, so the repeat is inexcusable. If the real gap is ten minutes inside a single redraft, the point is different and weaker -- the two errors are one drafting act, not two separated by reflection, and the remedy that follows from that is 'measure before promoting ANY reviewer claim in a draft', not 'remember yesterday's lesson'. A later reader auditing this file's honesty finds a wall-clock claim the artifacts in .harness/review refute, in the one paragraph whose entire value is that it is candid about the author's own failures, which discounts the candid parts that are true. Same class as the '203,911,796 ns' precision this task already corrected twice: a number stated more confidently than it was established.

findings.title: The entry's round numbers are offset by one from review_rounds.py, and the totals coincide, which hides it
findings.detail: The entry narrates rounds 1-4. review_rounds.py counts a round as a distinct staged hash recorded FOR THE TASK, and the entry's round 1 -- the review of these same three rows -- is filed under task M4.35, at hash 2853f985 (both verdicts say "task": "M4.35"). So the script's M4.38 set is {9a50b5d0, a6f08958, b699a7d0, this hash} and the entry's is {2853f985, 9a50b5d0, a6f08958, b699a7d0}: same size, different members. After this round lands, `scripts/review_rounds.py --for-task M4.38` prints 4 and the entry narrates 4, so a reader reconciling them concludes every round is accounted for, while in fact round 1 lives under another ID and the round this line was added in is narrated nowhere. A second, checkable consequence: `--for-task M4.35` already prints 1, so M4.35 inherits a review round from a commit that only FILED it, and the cap bites one round earlier when someone implements it. The done row explains the ID split; the cap argument, which is the document a future session reads when it asks why this task ran long, does not.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.35 is picked up, its implementation is reviewed twice, and the gate refuses at what the implementer believes is round 2 of 2 because the counter has been carrying a round since this docs commit. The implementer reads baselines/review.txt for M4.35, finds no entry, reads the M4.38 entry, and it says nothing about round 1 having been recorded under M4.35 -- so the inherited round looks like a gate defect rather than an artifact of the ID split, and the response is likely to be a cap argument written to explain a round nobody in that session performed.

findings.title: PRE-EXISTING, carried: M4.36 says 'both round-2 reviewers measured' the latch pin -- one of them derived it, and the new baselines line is careful where the row is not
findings.detail: Recorded because this round's remit is the accuracy of measurement attribution and this is the same error class the new entry is about; NOT a request to fix, and it already carries passes from rounds 3 and 4. M4.36 reads 'THE PIN MUST BE INTERRUPT-PROOF, and both round-2 reviewers measured that getting this wrong pins NOTHING'. I measured it (9a50b5d0/T3: both variants run, latch survives, semaphore kills, ~150 ms). The production reviewer's R2-2 is a derivation -- line numbers, 'If the pin is a plain CountDownLatch.await(), that interrupt releases the committer', no run, no output, no numbers -- and that reviewer distinguishes the two carefully elsewhere in the same verdict ('NOT VERIFIED by running the pre-round-7 code' in R2-1, and an explicit 'Re-measured here: ... 210,625,821 ns' in R2-3). The new baselines line does NOT repeat this: it says only 'measured both ways' for round 2 and reserves 'both reviewers measured it independently' for round 3, where it is true of both records.
findings.failure_scenario: A session implementing M4.36 reads 'both round-2 reviewers measured' and treats the interrupt-proof-pin requirement as doubly established, so if its own latch-based red record refuses to go red it looks for the error in its fixture rather than reconsidering the claim. More corrosively, the row promoting a derivation to a measurement is the exact act the entry beside it calls the root cause of rounds 2 and 3 -- 'a review comment is a hypothesis; a backlog row is a prescription, and the measurement belongs between them' -- so the lesson and its counter-example ship in one commit.
